transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Lagos, Nigeria at 2026-01-20 11:57 WAT (UTC+0100) (2026-01-20T10:57:00Z in UTC), at latitude 6.5244 degrees and longitude 3.3792 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 59.542 degrees and its azimuth is 151.107 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 47.814 degrees and its azimuth is 124.404 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 2.74 percent illuminated, 19.022 degrees from the Sun, and 385267.8 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be completely honest with you: **No, you will not be able to see the Moon with your unaided eyes right now.**

While your app is correct that the Moon is physically above the horizon, there are three major factors working against you in this specific scenario:

### 1. The "Daylight Washout"
The most significant hurdle is the Sun. With the Sun at an altitude of nearly 60 degrees, it is very high in the sky. Because the Moon is only 19 degrees away from the Sun, it is located in the same general area of the sky. The atmosphere is currently scattering a massive amount of sunlight (Rayleigh scattering), creating a bright blue sky that completely overwhelms the faint light of a thin crescent.

### 2. The Phase (2.74% Illumination)
At only 2.74% illumination, the Moon is a very "thin" crescent. Even on a perfectly clear night, a crescent this small is much harder to see than a half-moon or a full moon. During the day, the "dark" part of the Moon is invisible, and the tiny sliver of illuminated part is simply not bright enough to compete with the surrounding blue of the atmosphere.

### 3. The Contrast
For an object to be visible to the human eye, it must have enough contrast against the background. Because the Moon is so close to the Sun in your current sky coordinates, it is essentially "lost" in the glare. It would be like trying to see a dim flashlight held up against a stadium floodlight from a distance.

**The Verdict:**
Even though the Moon is technically "there," it is currently drowned out by the brilliance of the day. You would likely need a pair of high-powered binoculars or a telescope to pick it out from the blue, and even then, it would be a challenge!
